blocks.c: Here is what I had lost after two trips down, as best I could establish, by sitting in a stairwell for two hours going through my own head like a man going through a burgled flat:

items: The name of the street I grew up on. Not the street. The name.
Whatever it was I used to hum. I know I hummed. There was a thing I hummed.

blocks.c: Three items, and only the first one had I noticed at the time.
Wen made me write them in the front of the log, not the back, on a page she made me title in capitals: OUTSTANDING.
"Front of the book," she said. "Always the front. The back is for messages, the margins are for warnings, the front is for debt. You want it to see the debt page every single time it opens the book."
"It reads everything you write. That's the deal. That's why rule one works." She stood up and stretched. "Now the hard part."

"You're going to go back up and do a normal shift," said Wen. "Four walks. Log everything. Don't come down. Don't do anything clever. And in three days, on the twenty-first, you're going to come down here at exactly 03:14 with both books and I'm going to show you the inventory."

"Because the lease renews every fifty-one years," she said, "and the last renewal was on the twenty-first of March, 1974, and I have been waiting thirty-one years to have somebody up top who can still sign their own name."
